meta.topic: 三大收敛定理、Riemann 与 Lebesgue、L^p 空间

zh: 设 $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ 为测度空间，$f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ 可测，且 $$0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots,\qquad f_n\uparrow f\ \text{a.e.}$$ 则 $f=\sup_n f_n$ a.e. 可测，允许取 $+\infty$。单调收敛定理（Levi 定理）断言 $$\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_X f_n\,d\mu=\int_X f\,d\mu,$$ 两端都在 $[0,+\infty]$ 中取值。定理不要求 $\mu(X)<+\infty$，不要求 $f_n$ 或 $f$ 可积；以下论证都在使单调性与收敛同时成立的那个全测集上进行，零测集上的取值不影响积分。

先证不需要技巧的一半。由 $f_n\le f$ a.e. 与积分的单调性，对每个 $n$ 有 $\int_X f_n\,d\mu\le\int_X f\,d\mu$，故 $$\limsup_{n\to\infty}\int_X f_n\,d\mu\le\int_X f\,d\mu.$$ 于是只剩反向不等式 $\int_X f\,d\mu\le\liminf_n\int_X f_n\,d\mu$。这一步完全在 $[0,+\infty]$ 中进行，不需要可积性。反向不等式并不是自动的：当 $\int f=+\infty$ 时，它正是结论 $\int f_n\to+\infty$；下文的简单函数逼近同时覆盖有限与无限两种情形。作为两端都为 $+\infty$ 的例子，在 $\mathbb R$ 上取 $f_n=\chi_{[-n,n]}$，则 $f_n\uparrow1$，而 $\int f_n=2n\to+\infty=\int1$。

反向不等式用「非负简单函数从下方逼近 $f$」来证。取非负简单函数 $$s=\sum_{k=1}^m a_k\chi_{A_k}\le f,\qquad 0\le a_k<+\infty,$$ 其中 $A_k$ 两两不交可测；再取 $\alpha\in(0,1)$，令 $$A_n=\{x\in X:\ f_n(x)\ge\alpha s(x)\}.$$ 每个 $A_n$ 可测，且 $A_n\subseteq A_{n+1}$。若 $s(x)>0$，则 $f(x)\ge s(x)>\alpha s(x)$，由 $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ 知 $x$ 最终属于 $A_n$；若 $s(x)=0$，则 $x\in A_n$ 对一切 $n$ 成立。故 $\bigcup_n A_n=X$（至多相差一个零测集）。

在 $A_n$ 上 $f_n\ge\alpha s$，于是 $$\begin{aligned}\int_X f_n\,d\mu&\ge\int_{A_n}f_n\,d\mu\ge\alpha\int_{A_n}s\,d\mu\\&=\alpha\sum_{k=1}^m a_k\,\mu(A_k\cap A_n).\end{aligned}$$ 由 $A_n\uparrow X$ 与测度的下方连续性，$\mu(A_k\cap A_n)\uparrow\mu(A_k)$；$m$ 与各 $a_k$ 有限，故可逐项取极限，得 $$\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int_X f_n\,d\mu\ge\alpha\int_X s\,d\mu.$$ 再令 $\alpha\uparrow1$，得 $\liminf_n\int_X f_n\,d\mu\ge\int_X s\,d\mu$。

对一切满足 $0\le s\le f$ 的非负简单函数 $s$ 取上确界。非负可测函数的 Lebesgue 积分按定义就是 $$\int_X f\,d\mu=\sup\Bigl\{\int_X s\,d\mu:\ 0\le s\le f,\ s\ \text{为简单函数}\Bigr\},$$ 所以第 4 步给出 $\int_X f\,d\mu\le\liminf_n\int_X f_n\,d\mu$。与第 2 步合并：$$\int f\le\liminf_n\int f_n\le\limsup_n\int f_n\le\int f,$$ 三个不等号迫使 $\lim_n\int f_n=\int f$。证毕。

两个条件都不能省。(i) 单调性：在 $(0,1)$ 上取 $f_n=n\chi_{(0,1/n)}$。对每个 $x\in(0,1)$，当 $n>1/x$ 时 $x\notin(0,1/n)$，故 $f_n(x)\to0$ 处处成立；但 $$\int_0^1 f_n\,dx=n\cdot\frac1n=1,\qquad \int_0^1 0\,dx=0,$$ 结论失效。该序列非负，却不单调。(ii) 非负性（或可积下界）：在 $\mathbb R$ 上取 $f_n=-\chi_{[n,\infty)}$，则 $f_n\uparrow0$ 处处成立，但 $\int_{\mathbb R}f_n\,d\mu=-\infty\ne0=\int_{\mathbb R}0\,d\mu$；这里下界 $g\equiv-1$ 在 $\mathbb R$ 上不可积。若存在 $g\in L^1(\mu)$ 使 $f_n\ge g$ a.e.，对非负列 $f_n-g$ 用定理再减去有限的 $\int g$，结论即恢复。
en: Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable with $$0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots,\qquad f_n\uparrow f\ \text{a.e.}$$ Then $f=\sup_n f_n$ a.e. is measurable and may take $+\infty$. The monotone convergence theorem (Levi's theorem) states $$\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_X f_n\,d\mu=\int_X f\,d\mu,$$ with both sides in $[0,+\infty]$. No finite measure and no integrability of $f_n$ or $f$ is required; the argument is carried out on the full-measure set where monotonicity and convergence hold, and values on null sets do not affect integrals.

First the easy half. From $f_n\le f$ a.e. and monotonicity of the integral, $\int_X f_n\,d\mu\le\int_X f\,d\mu$ for every $n$, hence $$\limsup_{n\to\infty}\int_X f_n\,d\mu\le\int_X f\,d\mu.$$ It remains to prove the reverse inequality $\int_X f\,d\mu\le\liminf_n\int_X f_n\,d\mu$. This takes place entirely in $[0,+\infty]$, so no integrability is needed. The reverse inequality is not automatic: when $\int f=+\infty$ it is precisely the assertion $\int f_n\to+\infty$; the simple-function approximation below covers both the finite and the infinite case. As an example where both sides equal $+\infty$, on $\mathbb R$ take $f_n=\chi_{[-n,n]}$; then $f_n\uparrow1$ while $\int f_n=2n\to+\infty=\int1$.

The reverse inequality is proved by approximating $f$ from below by nonnegative simple functions. Take $$s=\sum_{k=1}^m a_k\chi_{A_k}\le f,\qquad 0\le a_k<+\infty,$$ with pairwise disjoint measurable $A_k$, and fix $\alpha\in(0,1)$. Set $$A_n=\{x\in X:\ f_n(x)\ge\alpha s(x)\}.$$ Each $A_n$ is measurable and $A_n\subseteq A_{n+1}$. If $s(x)>0$, then $f(x)\ge s(x)>\alpha s(x)$, and $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ forces $x\in A_n$ eventually; if $s(x)=0$, then $x\in A_n$ for every $n$. Hence $\bigcup_n A_n=X$ up to a null set.

On $A_n$ we have $f_n\ge\alpha s$, so $$\begin{aligned}\int_X f_n\,d\mu&\ge\int_{A_n}f_n\,d\mu\ge\alpha\int_{A_n}s\,d\mu\\&=\alpha\sum_{k=1}^m a_k\,\mu(A_k\cap A_n).\end{aligned}$$ Since $A_n\uparrow X$, continuity from below gives $\mu(A_k\cap A_n)\uparrow\mu(A_k)$; both $m$ and the $a_k$ are finite, so the limit passes through the finite sum: $$\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int_X f_n\,d\mu\ge\alpha\int_X s\,d\mu.$$ Letting $\alpha\uparrow1$ yields $\liminf_n\int_X f_n\,d\mu\ge\int_X s\,d\mu$.

Now take the supremum over all nonnegative simple $s$ with $0\le s\le f$. By definition of the Lebesgue integral of a nonnegative measurable function, $$\int_X f\,d\mu=\sup\Bigl\{\int_X s\,d\mu:\ 0\le s\le f,\ s\ \text{simple}\Bigr\},$$ so Step 4 gives $\int_X f\,d\mu\le\liminf_n\int_X f_n\,d\mu$. Combined with Step 2, $$\int f\le\liminf_n\int f_n\le\limsup_n\int f_n\le\int f,$$ and the three inequalities force $\lim_n\int f_n=\int f$. This completes the proof.

Neither hypothesis can be dropped. (i) Monotonicity: on $(0,1)$ take $f_n=n\chi_{(0,1/n)}$. For every $x\in(0,1)$, once $n>1/x$ we have $x\notin(0,1/n)$, so $f_n(x)\to0$ everywhere; but $$\int_0^1 f_n\,dx=n\cdot\frac1n=1,\qquad \int_0^1 0\,dx=0,$$ and the conclusion fails. The sequence is nonnegative but not increasing. (ii) Nonnegativity (or an integrable lower bound): on $\mathbb R$ take $f_n=-\chi_{[n,\infty)}$. Then $f_n\uparrow0$ everywhere, yet $\int_{\mathbb R}f_n\,d\mu=-\infty\ne0=\int_{\mathbb R}0\,d\mu$; here the lower bound $g\equiv-1$ is not integrable on $\mathbb R$. If some $g\in L^1(\mu)$ satisfies $f_n\ge g$ a.e., applying the theorem to the nonnegative sequence $f_n-g$ and subtracting the finite $\int g$ restores the conclusion.

zh: 设 $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ 可测（$n\ge1$）。令 $$\begin{aligned}g_k(x)&=\inf_{n\ge k}f_n(x),\\g(x)&=\liminf_{n\to\infty}f_n(x)=\sup_{k\ge1}g_k(x).\end{aligned}$$ 则每个 $g_k\ge0$ 可测，$g_k\uparrow g$，且对一切 $n\ge k$ 有 $g_k\le f_n$。法图引理断言 $$\int_X g\,d\mu\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int_X f_n\,d\mu,$$ 两端都在 $[0,+\infty]$ 中。它不要求 $f_n$ 收敛、不要求单调、不要求 $f_n$ 可积，也不要求 $\mu(X)<+\infty$。

对非负递增列 $(g_k)$ 用单调收敛定理，得 $\int g_k\uparrow\int g$。另一方面，固定 $k$ 时 $g_k\le f_n$ 对一切 $n\ge k$ 成立，由积分单调性 $$\int g_k\,d\mu\le\inf_{n\ge k}\int f_n\,d\mu.$$ 于是 $$\begin{aligned}\int g\,d\mu&=\lim_{k\to\infty}\int g_k\,d\mu\\&\le\lim_{k\to\infty}\inf_{n\ge k}\int f_n\,d\mu=\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int f_n\,d\mu.\end{aligned}$$ 所有量都在 $[0,+\infty]$ 中，比较与取极限都不涉及 $\infty-\infty$。

不等号可以严格。在 $\mathbb R$ 上取 $$f_n=n\,\chi_{(n,\,n+1/n)},\qquad n\ge1.$$ 固定 $x$：当 $n>x$ 时 $x\notin(n,n+1/n)$，故 $f_n(x)=0$ 最终恒成立，$\liminf_n f_n=0$，从而 $\int\liminf_n f_n=0$。但 $$\int_{\mathbb R}f_n\,d\mu=n\cdot\frac1n=1$$ 对一切 $n$ 成立，故 $\liminf_n\int f_n=1$。于是 $$0=\int_{\mathbb R}\liminf_n f_n\,d\mu<\liminf_n\int_{\mathbb R}f_n\,d\mu=1.$$ 质量 $1$ 随区间滑向无穷远，逐点极限看不见它。

非负性不能去掉。在 $\mathbb R$ 上取 $f_n=-\chi_{[n,n+1)}$。每个 $x$ 只属于有限多个 $[n,n+1)$，故 $f_n(x)\to0$ 处处成立，$\int\liminf f_n=0$；而 $\int f_n=-1$ 对一切 $n$ 成立，$\liminf\int f_n=-1$，于是 $0>-1$。此时 $f_n\ge-1$，但 $g\equiv-1$ 在 $\mathbb R$ 上不可积，正说明需要可积下界。一般版本：若 $f_n\ge g$ a.e. 且 $g\in L^1$，对 $f_n-g\ge0$ 用法图引理，得 $$\begin{aligned}\int(\liminf_n f_n-g)\,d\mu&\le\liminf_n\int(f_n-g)\,d\mu\\&=\liminf_n\int f_n\,d\mu-\int g\,d\mu.\end{aligned}$$ 移项即得原不等式。

在上方有可积控制时，得到方向相反的上极限版本。设 $f_n\le g$ a.e. 且 $g\in L^1$。对非负列 $g-f_n\ge0$ 用法图引理：$$\int\liminf_n(g-f_n)\,d\mu\le\liminf_n\int(g-f_n)\,d\mu.$$ 左边 $=\int g\,d\mu-\int\limsup_n f_n\,d\mu$，右边 $=\int g\,d\mu-\limsup_n\int f_n\,d\mu$。由于 $\int g<+\infty$，两边减去 $\int g$ 并变号，得 $$\limsup_{n\to\infty}\int f_n\,d\mu\le\int\limsup_{n\to\infty}f_n\,d\mu.$$ 方向与法图引理相反，可积控制不可省。

法图引理给的是不等式而非等式：即使 $f_n\to f$ a.e.，若没有非负性或可积下界，也只能在额外条件下推出 $\int f\le\liminf\int f_n$。准确地说，若 $f_n\ge0$ a.e.（或 $f_n\ge g$ 且 $g\in L^1$）且 $f_n\to f$ a.e.，则 $\int f\le\liminf\int f_n$；等号需要额外条件（单调性，或可积控制）。它的主要用途有二。(i) 证明控制收敛定理：若 $|f_n-f|\le2g$ 且 $g\in L^1$，对 $2g-|f_n-f|\ge0$ 用法图引理即得 $\limsup\int|f_n-f|\le0$。(ii) 积分对 a.e. 收敛具有下半连续性：在非负性（或可积下界）下，$f_n\to f$ a.e. 时 $\int f\le\liminf\int f_n$，这是变分法中取极限的标准估计。最后注意「$f_n\ge0$」与「$f_n$ 可积」是两件事，法图引理允许 $\int f_n=+\infty$。
en: Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for $n\ge1$. Set $$\begin{aligned}g_k(x)&=\inf_{n\ge k}f_n(x),\\g(x)&=\liminf_{n\to\infty}f_n(x)=\sup_{k\ge1}g_k(x).\end{aligned}$$ Then each $g_k\ge0$ is measurable, $g_k\uparrow g$, and $g_k\le f_n$ for every $n\ge k$. Fatou's lemma states $$\int_X g\,d\mu\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int_X f_n\,d\mu,$$ with both sides in $[0,+\infty]$. It requires neither convergence, nor monotonicity, nor integrability of $f_n$, nor $\mu(X)<+\infty$.

Apply monotone convergence to the nonnegative increasing sequence $(g_k)$: $\int g_k\uparrow\int g$. On the other hand, for fixed $k$ we have $g_k\le f_n$ for every $n\ge k$, so monotonicity of the integral gives $$\int g_k\,d\mu\le\inf_{n\ge k}\int f_n\,d\mu.$$ Hence $$\begin{aligned}\int g\,d\mu&=\lim_{k\to\infty}\int g_k\,d\mu\\&\le\lim_{k\to\infty}\inf_{n\ge k}\int f_n\,d\mu=\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int f_n\,d\mu.\end{aligned}$$ All quantities lie in $[0,+\infty]$, so neither the comparison nor the limit involves $\infty-\infty$.

The inequality can be strict. On $\mathbb R$ take $$f_n=n\,\chi_{(n,\,n+1/n)},\qquad n\ge1.$$ For fixed $x$, once $n>x$ we have $x\notin(n,n+1/n)$, so $f_n(x)=0$ eventually and $\liminf_n f_n=0$; hence $\int\liminf_n f_n=0$. But $$\int_{\mathbb R}f_n\,d\mu=n\cdot\frac1n=1$$ for every $n$, so $\liminf_n\int f_n=1$. Thus $$0=\int_{\mathbb R}\liminf_n f_n\,d\mu<\liminf_n\int_{\mathbb R}f_n\,d\mu=1.$$ A unit of mass slides off to infinity and is invisible in the pointwise limit.

Nonnegativity cannot be dropped. On $\mathbb R$ take $f_n=-\chi_{[n,n+1)}$. Each $x$ belongs to only finitely many intervals $[n,n+1)$, so $f_n(x)\to0$ everywhere and $\int\liminf f_n=0$; however $\int f_n=-1$ for every $n$, so $\liminf\int f_n=-1$ and $0>-1$. Here $f_n\ge-1$, but $g\equiv-1$ is not integrable on $\mathbb R$, which is exactly why an integrable lower bound is needed. General version: if $f_n\ge g$ a.e. with $g\in L^1$, apply the lemma to $f_n-g\ge0$: $$\begin{aligned}\int(\liminf_n f_n-g)\,d\mu&\le\liminf_n\int(f_n-g)\,d\mu\\&=\liminf_n\int f_n\,d\mu-\int g\,d\mu.\end{aligned}$$ Rearranging gives the claim.

With an integrable upper bound one obtains the reverse direction. Suppose $f_n\le g$ a.e. with $g\in L^1$. Apply Fatou to the nonnegative sequence $g-f_n\ge0$: $$\int\liminf_n(g-f_n)\,d\mu\le\liminf_n\int(g-f_n)\,d\mu.$$ The left side is $\int g\,d\mu-\int\limsup_n f_n\,d\mu$, the right side is $\int g\,d\mu-\limsup_n\int f_n\,d\mu$. Since $\int g<+\infty$, subtracting $\int g$ and changing signs gives $$\limsup_{n\to\infty}\int f_n\,d\mu\le\int\limsup_{n\to\infty}f_n\,d\mu.$$ The direction is opposite to Fatou's lemma, and the integrable domination is indispensable.

Fatou's lemma gives an inequality, not an identity: even if $f_n\to f$ a.e., without nonnegativity or an integrable lower bound one cannot conclude $\int f\le\liminf\int f_n$. Precisely, if $f_n\ge0$ a.e. (or $f_n\ge g$ with $g\in L^1$) and $f_n\to f$ a.e., then $\int f\le\liminf\int f_n$; equality needs extra hypotheses (monotonicity, or integrable domination). It has two main uses. (i) Proof of dominated convergence: if $|f_n-f|\le2g$ with $g\in L^1$, applying Fatou to $2g-|f_n-f|\ge0$ gives $\limsup\int|f_n-f|\le0$. (ii) Lower semicontinuity of the integral: under nonnegativity (or an integrable lower bound), $f_n\to f$ a.e. implies $\int f\le\liminf\int f_n$, the standard estimate when passing to limits in the calculus of variations. Finally, $f_n\ge0$ and $f_n$ integrable are separate matters: Fatou's lemma allows $\int f_n=+\infty$.

zh: 设 $f_n,f$ 可测，且 $f_n\to f$ a.e.；又设存在可测函数 $g\in L^1(\mu)$，使 $$|f_n(x)|\le g(x)\quad\text{对一切 }n\ge1\text{ 及 a.e. }x.$$ 三个要点：同一个 $g$ 控制整个序列；不等式对所有 $n$ 成立；$g$ 必须可积，即 $\int_X g\,d\mu<+\infty$。结论是 $f\in L^1$、$|f|\le g$ a.e.，并且 $$\begin{aligned}\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_X f_n\,d\mu&=\int_X f\,d\mu,\\\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_X|f_n-f|\,d\mu&=0.\end{aligned}$$
在使 $f_n\to f$ 且 $|f_n|\le g$ 对所有 $n$ 同时成立的全测集上取极限，得 $|f|\le g$ a.e.。又 $f$ 已假设可测。于是 $$\int_X|f|\,d\mu\le\int_X g\,d\mu<+\infty,$$ 即 $f\in L^1$；并且 $|f_n-f|\le|f_n|+|f|\le2g$ a.e.。这个界是下一步的出发点。

令 $h_n=2g-|f_n-f|$。由第 2 步，$h_n\ge0$ a.e. 且可测。对 $(h_n)$ 用法图引理：$$\int_X\liminf_{n\to\infty}h_n\,d\mu\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int_X h_n\,d\mu.$$ 因 $|f_n-f|\to0$ a.e.，左边 $=\int_X2g\,d\mu$；右边 $=\int_X2g\,d\mu-\limsup_n\int_X|f_n-f|\,d\mu$，这里用到 $\int2g<+\infty$ 才能拆分。故 $$\int_X2g\,d\mu\le\int_X2g\,d\mu-\limsup_{n\to\infty}\int_X|f_n-f|\,d\mu,$$ 即 $\limsup_n\int_X|f_n-f|\,d\mu\le0$。

由于 $\int_X|f_n-f|\,d\mu\ge0$，第 3 步的 $\limsup\le0$ 迫使 $$\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_X|f_n-f|\,d\mu=0,$$ 即 $f_n\to f$ 在 $L^1$ 中。再由 $$0\le\Bigl|\int_X f_n\,d\mu-\int_X f\,d\mu\Bigr|\le\int_X|f_n-f|\,d\mu$$ 得 $\int f_n\to\int f$。同理，反向三角不等式 $\bigl|\|f_n\|_1-\|f\|_1\bigr|\le\|f_n-f\|_1$ 说明范数也收敛。

没有可积控制时结论会失败。在 $\mathbb R$ 上取 $f_n=\chi_{[n,n+1)}$：对每个 $x$，当 $n>x$ 时 $f_n(x)=0$，故 $f_n\to0$ 处处成立；但 $$\int_{\mathbb R}f_n\,d\mu=\mu([n,n+1))=1$$ 对一切 $n$ 成立，故 $\int f_n\not\to0$。这里 $\sup_n|f_n|=\chi_{[1,\infty)}$，任何满足 $g\ge\sup_n|f_n|$ a.e. 的 $g$ 都有 $\int g\ge\mu([1,\infty))=+\infty$，故不存在可积控制函数；可见「逐点极限有限」远远不够。另一种失效方式是质量集中：$f_n=n\chi_{(0,1/n)}$ 在 $(0,1)$ 上也逐点趋于 $0$，而 $\int f_n=1$，其上确界在 $0$ 附近不可积。

两个常用推论。(i) 有界收敛定理：若 $\mu(X)<+\infty$ 且 $|f_n|\le M$ a.e.，取常数 $g\equiv M$，则 $\int_X g\,d\mu=M\mu(X)<+\infty$，控制收敛定理适用。(ii) 广义控制收敛：若 $f_n\to f$ a.e.、$f$ 可测、$|f_n|\le g_n$、$g_n\to g$ a.e.、$g_n,g\in L^1$ 且 $\int g_n\to\int g$，则仍有 $\int f_n\to\int f$。此时控制函数随 $n$ 变化，必须额外假定控制质量不逃逸；仅有逐点 $g_n\to g$ 不够。应用原定理时逐条核对：a.e. 收敛、同一个可积 $g$、不等式对所有充分大的 $n$ 成立。
en: Let $f_n,f$ be measurable with $f_n\to f$ a.e., and suppose there is a measurable $g\in L^1(\mu)$ such that $$|f_n(x)|\le g(x)\quad\text{for all }n\ge1\text{ and a.e. }x.$$ Three points matter: one and the same $g$ dominates the whole sequence; the inequality holds for every $n$; and $g$ is integrable, $\int_X g\,d\mu<+\infty$. The conclusion is $f\in L^1$, $|f|\le g$ a.e., and $$\begin{aligned}\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_X f_n\,d\mu&=\int_X f\,d\mu,\\\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_X|f_n-f|\,d\mu&=0.\end{aligned}$$

On the full-measure set where $f_n\to f$ and $|f_n|\le g$ hold for all $n$, passing to the limit gives $|f|\le g$ a.e. Moreover $f$ is measurable by hypothesis. Hence $$\int_X|f|\,d\mu\le\int_X g\,d\mu<+\infty,$$ so $f\in L^1$, and $|f_n-f|\le|f_n|+|f|\le2g$ a.e. This bound is the starting point of the next step.

Set $h_n=2g-|f_n-f|$. By Step 2, $h_n\ge0$ a.e. and measurable. Fatou's lemma applied to $(h_n)$ gives $$\int_X\liminf_{n\to\infty}h_n\,d\mu\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int_X h_n\,d\mu.$$ Since $|f_n-f|\to0$ a.e., the left side equals $\int_X2g\,d\mu$; the right side equals $\int_X2g\,d\mu-\limsup_n\int_X|f_n-f|\,d\mu$, where $\int2g<+\infty$ is needed to split. Hence $$\int_X2g\,d\mu\le\int_X2g\,d\mu-\limsup_{n\to\infty}\int_X|f_n-f|\,d\mu,$$ that is, $\limsup_n\int_X|f_n-f|\,d\mu\le0$.

Since $\int_X|f_n-f|\,d\mu\ge0$, the bound $\limsup\le0$ from Step 3 forces $$\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_X|f_n-f|\,d\mu=0,$$ i.e. $f_n\to f$ in $L^1$. Then $$0\le\Bigl|\int_X f_n\,d\mu-\int_X f\,d\mu\Bigr|\le\int_X|f_n-f|\,d\mu$$ gives $\int f_n\to\int f$. Likewise the reverse triangle inequality $\bigl|\|f_n\|_1-\|f\|_1\bigr|\le\|f_n-f\|_1$ shows that the norms converge.

Without integrable domination the conclusion can fail. On $\mathbb R$ take $f_n=\chi_{[n,n+1)}$: for each $x$, $f_n(x)=0$ once $n>x$, so $f_n\to0$ everywhere; but $$\int_{\mathbb R}f_n\,d\mu=\mu([n,n+1))=1$$ for every $n$, so $\int f_n\not\to0$. Here $\sup_n|f_n|=\chi_{[1,\infty)}$, and any $g\ge\sup_n|f_n|$ a.e. satisfies $\int g\ge\mu([1,\infty))=+\infty$, so no integrable dominator exists; a finite pointwise limit is far from enough. A second mechanism is concentration: $f_n=n\chi_{(0,1/n)}$ on $(0,1)$ also tends to $0$ pointwise while $\int f_n=1$, and its pointwise supremum is not integrable near $0$.

Two standard corollaries. (i) Bounded convergence: if $\mu(X)<+\infty$ and $|f_n|\le M$ a.e., take the constant $g\equiv M$; then $\int_X g\,d\mu=M\mu(X)<+\infty$ and dominated convergence applies. (ii) Generalized dominated convergence: if $f_n\to f$ a.e., $f$ is measurable, $|f_n|\le g_n$, $g_n\to g$ a.e., $g_n,g\in L^1$ and $\int g_n\to\int g$, then still $\int f_n\to\int f$. Here the dominators vary with $n$, and the extra hypothesis prevents the dominating mass from escaping; pointwise $g_n\to g$ alone is insufficient. When applying the original theorem, check each hypothesis: a.e. convergence, one integrable $g$, and the bound for all sufficiently large $n$.

zh: 设 $f$ 在 $[a,b]$ 上有界。对分割 $P:a=x_0<x_1<\cdots<x_n=b$，记 $$m_i=\inf_{[x_{i-1},x_i]}f,\qquad M_i=\sup_{[x_{i-1},x_i]}f,$$ 并作 Darboux 上下和 $$\begin{aligned}L(f,P)&=\sum_{i=1}^n m_i\Delta x_i,\\U(f,P)&=\sum_{i=1}^n M_i\Delta x_i.\end{aligned}$$ 常义黎曼可积是指 $\sup_P L(f,P)=\inf_P U(f,P)=:I$。要证：此时 $f$ 也 Lebesgue 可积，且 $\int_{[a,b]}f\,d\mu=I$。

先用 Lebesgue 判据取得可测性。有界函数 $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ 黎曼可积，当且仅当其不连续点集 $D_f$ 是零测集。记振幅 $$\omega_f(x)=\inf_{\delta>0}\sup_{y,z\in(x-\delta,x+\delta)\cap[a,b]}|f(y)-f(z)|,$$ 则 $f$ 在 $x$ 连续 $\iff\omega_f(x)=0$，且 $D_f=\bigcup_{k\ge1}\{\omega_f\ge1/k\}$。若 $U(f,P)-L(f,P)<\delta$，则振幅 $\ge1/k$ 的那些小区间总长 $<k\delta$；再加上有限个分点的小邻域，即知紧集 $\{\omega_f\ge1/k\}$ 可被总长任意小的有限个区间覆盖，从而是零测集；反之若 $D_f$ 零测，取总长任意小的开区间覆盖 $D_f$；在剩下的紧集上 $f$ 处处连续、因而一致连续。取足够细的分割，未落入覆盖的小区间上振幅任意小，落入覆盖的小区间总长任意小，故 $U-L$ 任意小。这就完成了判据的证明。于是黎曼可积的 $f$ 满足 $D_f$ 零测；$f$ 在 $D_f^c$ 上连续，在零测集 $D_f$ 上任意改值后仍 Lebesgue 可测。

对固定分割 $P$，定义阶梯函数 $$\begin{aligned}l_P&=\sum_{i=1}^n m_i\chi_{(x_{i-1},x_i]},\\u_P&=\sum_{i=1}^n M_i\chi_{(x_{i-1},x_i]}.\end{aligned}$$ 则 $l_P\le f\le u_P$ 于 $(a,b]$（端点无影响）。阶梯函数的 Lebesgue 积分等于 $$\begin{aligned}\int_{[a,b]}l_P\,d\mu&=\sum_{i=1}^n m_i\Delta x_i=L(f,P),\\\int_{[a,b]}u_P\,d\mu&=U(f,P).\end{aligned}$$ 因此对每个 $P$，$$\int_{[a,b]}l_P\,d\mu\le\int_*f\le\int^*f\le\int_{[a,b]}u_P\,d\mu,$$ 其中 $\int_*$、$\int^*$ 分别为 Lebesgue 下积分与上积分。

由黎曼可积性，$I=\sup_P L(f,P)=\inf_P U(f,P)$。在第 3 步的不等式中对 $P$ 取上确界与下确界：$$I=\sup_P L(f,P)\le\int_*f\le\int^*f\le\inf_P U(f,P)=I.$$ 于是 $\int_*f=\int^*f=I$。$f$ 已由第 2 步保证可测且有界；有界可测函数的下积分等于上积分时，它 Lebesgue 可积，积分就是这个公共值。因此 $$\int_{[a,b]}f\,d\mu=I=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx,$$ 即「黎曼可积 $\Rightarrow$ 勒贝格可积且积分相等」。

Dirichlet 函数说明逆命题不成立。取 $f=\chi_{\mathbb Q\cap[0,1]}$。它有界，但对任意 $x\in[0,1]$ 与任意 $\delta>0$，区间 $(x-\delta,x+\delta)$ 内既有有理数又有无理数，故 $f$ 在 $x$ 处的振幅为 $1$，从而 $D_f=[0,1]$，$\mu(D_f)=1\ne0$；由第 2 步 $f$ 不黎曼可积（也可直接看：任何分割的上和恒为 $1$、下和恒为 $0$）。另一方面 $\mathbb Q\cap[0,1]$ 可数，是零测集，故 $f=0$ a.e.，Lebesgue 积分存在且 $$\int_{[0,1]}f\,d\mu=0.$$ 所以有界函数中黎曼可积严格强于勒贝格可积。

常义与反常必须分开。设 $f\ge0$ 在 $[a,+\infty)$ 上局部黎曼可积。若反常积分 $\lim_{b\to+\infty}\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$ 存在且有限，则 $b\mapsto\int_a^b f$ 单调递增，由单调收敛定理 $$\int_{[a,+\infty)}f\,d\mu=\lim_{b\to+\infty}\int_a^b f(x)\,dx<+\infty,$$ 两种积分一致；绝对收敛的情形对 $|f|$ 用上述非负结论、再对 $f\chi_{[a,b]}$ 用控制收敛定理，结论同样成立；有限端点处，若非负函数在 $(a,b]$ 上的反常积分有限，同样由单调收敛定理得到 $f\in L^1$ 且值相等。条件收敛则不然（$x=0$ 处按连续延拓取值）：$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^{+\infty}\frac{\sin x}{x}\,dx&=\frac\pi2\quad(\text{反常黎曼收敛}),\\\int_0^{+\infty}\Bigl|\frac{\sin x}{x}\Bigr|\,dx&=+\infty.\end{aligned}$$ 因为 $\int_{n\pi}^{(n+1)\pi}\frac{|\sin x|}{x}dx\ge\frac{2}{(n+1)\pi}$，求和得调和级数发散。故 $\sin x/x\notin L^1$；事实上正瓣与负瓣各自的积分都发散（同样的调和级数下界），所以正、负部都为 $+\infty$，Lebesgue 积分不是有限的 $\pm\infty$，而是无定义。若只需说明它不是 Lebesgue 可积，则 $\notin L^1$ 已足够。结论：常义黎曼可积 $\Rightarrow$ Lebesgue 可积且同值；反常积分只在非负或绝对收敛时才与 Lebesgue 积分一致。
en: Let $f$ be bounded on $[a,b]$. For a partition $P:a=x_0<x_1<\cdots<x_n=b$, put $$m_i=\inf_{[x_{i-1},x_i]}f,\qquad M_i=\sup_{[x_{i-1},x_i]}f,$$ and form the Darboux sums $$\begin{aligned}L(f,P)&=\sum_{i=1}^n m_i\Delta x_i,\\U(f,P)&=\sum_{i=1}^n M_i\Delta x_i.\end{aligned}$$ Proper Riemann integrability means $\sup_P L(f,P)=\inf_P U(f,P)=:I$. We prove that then $f$ is Lebesgue integrable and $\int_{[a,b]}f\,d\mu=I$.

First use Lebesgue's criterion to obtain measurability. A bounded $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable if and only if its set of discontinuities $D_f$ is null. Define the oscillation $$\omega_f(x)=\inf_{\delta>0}\sup_{y,z\in(x-\delta,x+\delta)\cap[a,b]}|f(y)-f(z)|.$$ Then $f$ is continuous at $x$ iff $\omega_f(x)=0$, and $D_f=\bigcup_{k\ge1}\{\omega_f\ge1/k\}$. If $U(f,P)-L(f,P)<\delta$, the subintervals on which the oscillation is $\ge1/k$ have total length $<k\delta$; adding small neighborhoods of the finitely many partition points shows that each compact set $\{\omega_f\ge1/k\}$ can be covered by finitely many intervals of arbitrarily small total length and is null; conversely, if $D_f$ is null, cover it by open intervals of arbitrarily small total length; on the remaining compact set $f$ is continuous everywhere, hence uniformly continuous. For a sufficiently fine partition, the subintervals meeting that compact set have arbitrarily small oscillation, while those contained in the cover have arbitrarily small total length, so $U-L$ is arbitrarily small. This proves the criterion. Thus a Riemann integrable $f$ has $D_f$ null; $f$ is continuous off $D_f$, and redefining it arbitrarily on the null set $D_f$ leaves it Lebesgue measurable.

For a fixed partition $P$ define step functions $$\begin{aligned}l_P&=\sum_{i=1}^n m_i\chi_{(x_{i-1},x_i]},\\u_P&=\sum_{i=1}^n M_i\chi_{(x_{i-1},x_i]},\end{aligned}$$ so that $l_P\le f\le u_P$ on $(a,b]$ (endpoints do not matter). Their Lebesgue integrals are $$\begin{aligned}\int_{[a,b]}l_P\,d\mu&=\sum_{i=1}^n m_i\Delta x_i=L(f,P),\\\int_{[a,b]}u_P\,d\mu&=U(f,P).\end{aligned}$$ Hence for every $P$, $$\int_{[a,b]}l_P\,d\mu\le\int_*f\le\int^*f\le\int_{[a,b]}u_P\,d\mu,$$ where $\int_*$ and $\int^*$ denote the lower and upper Lebesgue integrals.

By Riemann integrability, $I=\sup_P L(f,P)=\inf_P U(f,P)$. Taking the supremum over $P$ on the left and the infimum on the right in Step 3 gives $$I=\sup_P L(f,P)\le\int_*f\le\int^*f\le\inf_P U(f,P)=I.$$ Therefore $\int_*f=\int^*f=I$. Step 2 already gives that $f$ is measurable and bounded; for a bounded measurable function, equality of its lower and upper integrals means it is Lebesgue integrable, with the common value as integral. Thus $$\int_{[a,b]}f\,d\mu=I=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx,$$ which is the precise sense in which Riemann integrability implies Lebesgue integrability with the same value.

The Dirichlet function shows that the converse fails. Take $f=\chi_{\mathbb Q\cap[0,1]}$. It is bounded, but for every $x\in[0,1]$ and every $\delta>0$ the interval $(x-\delta,x+\delta)$ contains both rationals and irrationals, so the oscillation at $x$ is $1$; hence $D_f=[0,1]$ and $\mu(D_f)=1\ne0$, so $f$ is not Riemann integrable by Step 2 (directly: every upper sum is $1$ and every lower sum is $0$). On the other hand $\mathbb Q\cap[0,1]$ is countable and null, so $f=0$ a.e. and $$\int_{[0,1]}f\,d\mu=0.$$ Among bounded functions, Riemann integrability is therefore strictly stronger than Lebesgue integrability.

Proper and improper Riemann integrals must be treated separately. Let $f\ge0$ on $[a,+\infty)$ be locally Riemann integrable. If the improper integral $\lim_{b\to+\infty}\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$ exists and is finite, then $b\mapsto\int_a^b f$ is nondecreasing, and monotone convergence gives $$\int_{[a,+\infty)}f\,d\mu=\lim_{b\to+\infty}\int_a^b f(x)\,dx<+\infty,$$ so the two integrals agree; for an absolutely convergent improper integral apply the nonnegative case to $|f|$ and then dominated convergence to $f\chi_{[a,b]}$; at a finite endpoint, if the improper integral of a nonnegative function on $(a,b]$ is finite, monotone convergence again gives $f\in L^1$ with the same value. Conditional convergence is different (with the continuous extension at $x=0$): $$\begin{aligned}\int_0^{+\infty}\frac{\sin x}{x}\,dx&=\frac\pi2\quad(\text{improper Riemann}),\\\int_0^{+\infty}\Bigl|\frac{\sin x}{x}\Bigr|\,dx&=+\infty.\end{aligned}$$ Because $\int_{n\pi}^{(n+1)\pi}\frac{|\sin x|}{x}dx\ge\frac{2}{(n+1)\pi}$ and the harmonic series diverges, the displayed integral is infinite; hence $\sin x/x\notin L^1$. In fact the positive and negative lobes each diverge by the same harmonic-series lower bound, so both the positive and negative parts are $+\infty$ and the Lebesgue integral is undefined, not merely infinite with a sign. If one only needs to say that it is not Lebesgue integrable, $\notin L^1$ is enough. In short: proper Riemann integrability implies Lebesgue integrability with the same value, while improper integrals agree with the Lebesgue integral only under nonnegativity or absolute convergence.

zh: 固定测度空间 $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ 与 $1\le p<+\infty$。可测函数 $f$ 属于 $L^p(\mu)$，是指 $$\int_X|f|^p\,d\mu<+\infty,$$ 此时定义 $p$ 范数 $\|f\|_p=\bigl(\int_X|f|^p\,d\mu\bigr)^{1/p}$。$p=\infty$ 时改用本性上确界 $$\|f\|_\infty=\operatorname{ess\,sup}|f|=\inf\{M\ge0:\mu(\{|f|>M\})=0\},$$ 并要求它有限。关键约定：$\|f\|_p=0$ 只推出 $f=0$ a.e.，所以 $L^p$ 的元素是 a.e. 相等的函数的等价类；不作这个认同，$\|\cdot\|_p$ 只是半范数，正定性不成立。

设 $1<p<+\infty$，$q=\frac{p}{p-1}$，则 $\frac1p+\frac1q=1$。由 Young 不等式 $ab\le\frac{a^p}{p}+\frac{b^q}{q}$（$a,b\ge0$），对 $$a=\frac{|f(x)|}{\|f\|_p},\qquad b=\frac{|g(x)|}{\|g\|_q}$$ 积分得 $$\frac{\int_X|fg|\,d\mu}{\|f\|_p\|g\|_q}\le\frac1p+\frac1q=1,$$ 即 Hölder 不等式 $\int_X|fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q$。若某个范数为 $0$ 或 $+\infty$，按平凡情形处理或用截断函数取极限。端点 $p=1,q=\infty$ 由 $|fg|\le\|g\|_\infty|f|$ a.e. 直接得到。

设 $1<p<+\infty$。由 $|f+g|^p\le(|f|+|g|)|f+g|^{p-1}$，对 $|f|$ 与 $|f+g|^{p-1}$ 用 Hölder（后者的共轭指数为 $q=\frac{p}{p-1}$）：$$\begin{aligned}\int_X|f+g|^p\,d\mu&\le\|f\|_p\Bigl(\int_X|f+g|^{(p-1)q}\,d\mu\Bigr)^{1/q}\\&\quad+\|g\|_p\Bigl(\int_X|f+g|^{(p-1)q}\,d\mu\Bigr)^{1/q}\\&=\bigl(\|f\|_p+\|g\|_p\bigr)\|f+g\|_p^{p-1}.\end{aligned}$$ 由 $|f+g|^p\le2^{p-1}(|f|^p+|g|^p)$ 知 $f+g\in L^p$，故 $\|f+g\|_p<+\infty$。若 $\|f+g\|_p=0$，三角不等式显然；否则两边除以 $\|f+g\|_p^{p-1}$，得 Minkowski 不等式 $\|f+g\|_p\le\|f\|_p+\|g\|_p$。$p=1$ 由 $|f+g|\le|f|+|g|$ 直接得到，$p=\infty$ 由本性上确界的次可加性得到。结合齐次性与正定性，$\|\cdot\|_p$ 是范数，$L^p$ 是赋范线性空间。

完备性（Riesz–Fischer）：设 $(f_n)$ 是 $L^p$ 中的 Cauchy 列，$1\le p<+\infty$。取子列使 $\|f_{n_{k+1}}-f_{n_k}\|_p\le2^{-k}$，令 $$g=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}|f_{n_{k+1}}-f_{n_k}|.$$ 由 Minkowski 不等式与单调收敛定理，$\|g\|_p\le\sum_k2^{-k}<+\infty$，故 $g<+\infty$ a.e.。于是级数 $f_{n_1}+\sum_k(f_{n_{k+1}}-f_{n_k})$ 在 $\mathbb R$ 中绝对收敛 a.e.，其和记为 $f$；则 $f$ 可测，且 $|f|\le|f_{n_1}|+g\in L^p$。记尾部 $R_k=\sum_{j\ge k}|f_{n_{j+1}}-f_{n_j}|$，则 $|f-f_{n_k}|\le R_k\le R_1$，且 $\|R_k\|_p\le2^{-k+1}\to0$；对 $|f-f_{n_k}|^p\le R_1^p\in L^1$ 用控制收敛定理，得 $\|f-f_{n_k}\|_p\to0$。Cauchy 列若有收敛子列则自身收敛，故 $L^p$ 完备，是 Banach 空间。$p=\infty$ 时同样的子列论证在零测集外给出一致收敛，$L^\infty$ 也完备。

$p=\infty$ 时范数是本性上确界：$$\|f\|_\infty=\inf\{M\ge0:\mu(\{|f|>M\})=0\}.$$ 它满足 $\|f\|_\infty=0\iff f=0$ a.e.，$\|fg\|_\infty\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_\infty$，$\|f+g\|_\infty\le\|f\|_\infty+\|g\|_\infty$。例如 $f=\chi_{\mathbb Q\cap[0,1]}$ 处处不连续，但 $f=0$ a.e.，故 $\|f\|_\infty=0$ 而不是 $1$——本性上确界忽略零测集。若 $f\in L^{p_0}$ 对某个 $p_0<+\infty$ 成立，则当 $p\to\infty$ 时 $\|f\|_p\to\|f\|_\infty$。若 $\|f\|_\infty=0$，则 $f=0$ a.e.，结论显然。若 $\|f\|_\infty=+\infty$，对任意 $M>0$，集合 $A_M=\{|f|>M\}$ 有有限正测度（否则 $\int|f|^{p_0}\ge M^{p_0}\mu(A_M)=+\infty$，与 $f\in L^{p_0}$ 矛盾），故 $$\|f\|_p\ge M\mu(A_M)^{1/p}\to M,$$ 令 $M\to\infty$ 得 $\|f\|_p\to+\infty$。以下设 $0<\|f\|_\infty<+\infty$。对 $0<\varepsilon<\|f\|_\infty$，集合 $A_\varepsilon=\{|f|>\|f\|_\infty-\varepsilon\}$ 有有限正测度，且 $$\begin{aligned}\Bigl(\int_X|f|^p\,d\mu\Bigr)^{1/p}&\ge\bigl(\|f\|_\infty-\varepsilon\bigr)\mu(A_\varepsilon)^{1/p}\\&\to\|f\|_\infty-\varepsilon.\end{aligned}$$ 再令 $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ 得下界。上界用插值：$p\ge p_0$ 时 $|f|^p\le\|f\|_\infty^{p-p_0}|f|^{p_0}$，故 $$\|f\|_p\le\|f\|_\infty^{1-p_0/p}\|f\|_{p_0}^{p_0/p}\to\|f\|_\infty.$$ 两边夹得结论。

设 $\mu(X)<+\infty$ 且 $1\le p<q\le\infty$。当 $q<+\infty$ 时，令 $r=q/p>1$，其共轭指数 $r'=q/(q-p)$；对 $|f|^p$ 与常数函数 $1\in L^{r'}(\mu)$ 用 Hölder：$$\int_X|f|^p\,d\mu\le\Bigl(\int_X|f|^q\,d\mu\Bigr)^{p/q}\mu(X)^{1-p/q},$$ 两边开 $p$ 次方得 $$\|f\|_p\le\mu(X)^{1/p-1/q}\|f\|_q.$$ 故 $L^q(\mu)\subseteq L^p(\mu)$：指数越大，空间越小。$q=\infty$ 时同理由 $\int|f|^p\le\|f\|_\infty^p\mu(X)$ 得 $\|f\|_p\le\mu(X)^{1/p}\|f\|_\infty$。有限测度不能丢：在 $(1,+\infty)$ 上 $1/x\in L^2\setminus L^1$；在 $(0,1)$ 上 $x^{-1/2}\in L^1\setminus L^2$，后者同时说明即使在有限测度空间，$L^1\subseteq L^2$ 也不成立，包含关系可以是严格的。
en: Fix a measure space $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $1\le p<+\infty$. A measurable $f$ belongs to $L^p(\mu)$ if $$\int_X|f|^p\,d\mu<+\infty,$$ and then its $p$-norm is $\|f\|_p=\bigl(\int_X|f|^p\,d\mu\bigr)^{1/p}$. For $p=\infty$ one uses the essential supremum $$\|f\|_\infty=\operatorname{ess\,sup}|f|=\inf\{M\ge0:\mu(\{|f|>M\})=0\},$$ required to be finite. Key convention: $\|f\|_p=0$ only implies $f=0$ a.e., so the elements of $L^p$ are a.e. equivalence classes of functions; without this identification $\|\cdot\|_p$ is only a seminorm and positive definiteness fails.

Let $1<p<+\infty$ and $q=\frac{p}{p-1}$, so $\frac1p+\frac1q=1$. Young's inequality $ab\le\frac{a^p}{p}+\frac{b^q}{q}$ for $a,b\ge0$, applied to $$a=\frac{|f(x)|}{\|f\|_p},\qquad b=\frac{|g(x)|}{\|g\|_q},$$ and integrated, gives $$\frac{\int_X|fg|\,d\mu}{\|f\|_p\|g\|_q}\le\frac1p+\frac1q=1,$$ i.e. Hölder's inequality $\int_X|fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q$. If one of the norms is $0$ or $+\infty$, the inequality is trivial or follows by truncation. The endpoint $p=1,q=\infty$ follows directly from $|fg|\le\|g\|_\infty|f|$ a.e.

Let $1<p<+\infty$. From $|f+g|^p\le(|f|+|g|)|f+g|^{p-1}$, apply Hölder to $|f|$ and $|f+g|^{p-1}$ (whose conjugate exponent is $q=\frac{p}{p-1}$): $$\begin{aligned}\int_X|f+g|^p\,d\mu&\le\|f\|_p\Bigl(\int_X|f+g|^{(p-1)q}\,d\mu\Bigr)^{1/q}\\&\quad+\|g\|_p\Bigl(\int_X|f+g|^{(p-1)q}\,d\mu\Bigr)^{1/q}\\&=\bigl(\|f\|_p+\|g\|_p\bigr)\|f+g\|_p^{p-1}.\end{aligned}$$ Since $|f+g|^p\le2^{p-1}(|f|^p+|g|^p)$, we have $f+g\in L^p$ and hence $\|f+g\|_p<+\infty$. If $\|f+g\|_p=0$ the triangle inequality is trivial; otherwise divide by $\|f+g\|_p^{p-1}$ to obtain Minkowski's inequality $\|f+g\|_p\le\|f\|_p+\|g\|_p$. The case $p=1$ is immediate from $|f+g|\le|f|+|g|$, and $p=\infty$ follows from subadditivity of the essential supremum. With homogeneity and positive definiteness, $\|\cdot\|_p$ is a norm and $L^p$ is a normed space.

Completeness (Riesz–Fischer): let $(f_n)$ be Cauchy in $L^p$, $1\le p<+\infty$. Choose a subsequence with $\|f_{n_{k+1}}-f_{n_k}\|_p\le2^{-k}$ and set $$g=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}|f_{n_{k+1}}-f_{n_k}|.$$ By Minkowski's inequality and monotone convergence, $\|g\|_p\le\sum_k2^{-k}<+\infty$, so $g<+\infty$ a.e. Hence the series $f_{n_1}+\sum_k(f_{n_{k+1}}-f_{n_k})$ converges absolutely a.e. in $\mathbb R$; denote its sum by $f$. Then $f$ is measurable and $|f|\le|f_{n_1}|+g\in L^p$. For the tail $R_k=\sum_{j\ge k}|f_{n_{j+1}}-f_{n_j}|$ we have $|f-f_{n_k}|\le R_k\le R_1$ and $\|R_k\|_p\le2^{-k+1}\to0$; dominated convergence applied to $|f-f_{n_k}|^p\le R_1^p\in L^1$ gives $\|f-f_{n_k}\|_p\to0$. A Cauchy sequence with a convergent subsequence converges, so $L^p$ is complete, hence a Banach space. For $p=\infty$ the same subsequence argument yields uniform convergence off a null set, so $L^\infty$ is complete as well.

For $p=\infty$ the norm is the essential supremum: $$\|f\|_\infty=\inf\{M\ge0:\mu(\{|f|>M\})=0\}.$$ It satisfies $\|f\|_\infty=0\iff f=0$ a.e., $\|fg\|_\infty\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_\infty$ and $\|f+g\|_\infty\le\|f\|_\infty+\|g\|_\infty$. For example $f=\chi_{\mathbb Q\cap[0,1]}$ is discontinuous everywhere, yet $f=0$ a.e., so $\|f\|_\infty=0$ rather than $1$: the essential supremum ignores null sets. If $f\in L^{p_0}$ for some $p_0<+\infty$, then $\|f\|_p\to\|f\|_\infty$ as $p\to\infty$. If $\|f\|_\infty=0$ then $f=0$ a.e. and the claim is trivial. If $\|f\|_\infty=+\infty$, then for every $M>0$ the set $A_M=\{|f|>M\}$ has finite positive measure (otherwise $\int|f|^{p_0}\ge M^{p_0}\mu(A_M)=+\infty$, contradicting $f\in L^{p_0}$), hence $$\|f\|_p\ge M\mu(A_M)^{1/p}\to M,$$ and letting $M\to\infty$ gives $\|f\|_p\to+\infty$. Now assume $0<\|f\|_\infty<+\infty$. For $0<\varepsilon<\|f\|_\infty$ the set $A_\varepsilon=\{|f|>\|f\|_\infty-\varepsilon\}$ has finite positive measure, and $$\begin{aligned}\Bigl(\int_X|f|^p\,d\mu\Bigr)^{1/p}&\ge\bigl(\|f\|_\infty-\varepsilon\bigr)\mu(A_\varepsilon)^{1/p}\\&\to\|f\|_\infty-\varepsilon.\end{aligned}$$ Let $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ for the lower bound. For the upper bound use interpolation: for $p\ge p_0$, $|f|^p\le\|f\|_\infty^{p-p_0}|f|^{p_0}$, so $$\|f\|_p\le\|f\|_\infty^{1-p_0/p}\|f\|_{p_0}^{p_0/p}\to\|f\|_\infty.$$ The two bounds give the claim.

Suppose $\mu(X)<+\infty$ and $1\le p<q\le\infty$. For $q<+\infty$ let $r=q/p>1$, with conjugate exponent $r'=q/(q-p)$; Hölder applied to $|f|^p$ and the constant function $1\in L^{r'}(\mu)$ gives $$\int_X|f|^p\,d\mu\le\Bigl(\int_X|f|^q\,d\mu\Bigr)^{p/q}\mu(X)^{1-p/q},$$ and taking $p$-th roots yields $$\|f\|_p\le\mu(X)^{1/p-1/q}\|f\|_q.$$ Hence $L^q(\mu)\subseteq L^p(\mu)$: the larger exponent gives the smaller space. For $q=\infty$, $\int|f|^p\le\|f\|_\infty^p\mu(X)$ gives $\|f\|_p\le\mu(X)^{1/p}\|f\|_\infty$. Finite measure is indispensable: on $(1,+\infty)$, $1/x\in L^2\setminus L^1$; on $(0,1)$, $x^{-1/2}\in L^1\setminus L^2$. The latter also shows that even with $\mu(X)<+\infty$ the inclusion $L^1\subseteq L^2$ fails, so the inclusion can be strict.
